entries.title: board.yaml is read per worktree though the board is one per hub
entries.brief: A pair with an older board.yaml re-renders README with the old types; move board.yaml beside fabric.yaml in _board
entries.body:
The board is one per hub (`<hub>/_board`), but its config, `board.yaml` (types, labels, README settings), is read from each worktree's own `_lyx/config/`.
Seen 2026-10-05: after the hub added the `feature` type in the prime's config, the landing of `lyx-skills-and-stencils` wrote to the board from its pair, whose copy predates the change, and re-rendered README with every `feature` note under "Other"; the hub re-rendered from the prime.
Every pair created before a vocabulary change does the same until it is torn down.

Precedent: `fabric.yaml` already lives once per repo at `<BoardDir>/_lyx/config/fabric.yaml`, because the junction set is a repo-wide fact every worktree reconciles against (`internal/fabricengine/doc.go`).
`board.yaml` describes the one board, so the same holds.

Proposal: `board.yaml` moves beside `fabric.yaml` in `_board/_lyx/config/`, and every `lyx board` verb reads it from there, whatever worktree it runs in.
Check which other config files are repo-wide facts the same way before generalizing; `config-overlay` is the general version, `config-reaches-parent` the related bug.

entries.title: Agents stop wrapping commands: stdin without a hook, a bare shed step
entries.brief: Give agent shells /dev/null stdin without a per-call hook; lyx shed step prints a short envelope so the driver runs the bare call
entries.body:
Agents wrap commands they have no reason to wrap.
Two symptoms of the one habit, merged from the notes `agent-stdin-hang` and `driver-step-clutter`.

## Stdin hang

Agents' Bash shells hung on stdin for up to 80 minutes, holding verify gates (`board-model` #361 on 2026-10-04; `orch-cycle-hardening` and `webster-audit-recovery` on 2026-10-05).

Cause (transcript study, 2026-10-05): the model, mostly Sonnet fork subagents, emits a bare `cat > /tmp/x;` or `python3 -;` with no input attached, often as a no-op (`cat > /tmp/x 2>/dev/null; true`); 54 such calls between 2026-09-24 and 2026-10-04.
The stored commands keep their newlines and no layer rewrote them.
No stencil shows the shape, and lyx cannot change the habit.

`3c5bfdb04` gave every Bash call `/dev/null` as stdin through a PreToolUse(Bash) rewrite hook (`bashStdinHookCommand`, `internal/shuttleengine/claudeengine/settings.go`), so such a command ends at once while heredocs, pipes and redirects still work.

- The operator dislikes hooks: each one delays every tool call.
  Give the agent's shell `/dev/null` as stdin without a per-call hook (e.g. how shuttle launches Claude Code, or `BASH_ENV`, checking it does not cut stdin from a script fed through a pipe), and drop the hook if one works.
  A timeout that ends the hang after the fact is not a fix.
- If no hook-free way works and the hook stays: it extracts the command with a `sed` regex taking the last `"command":"` key in the raw payload, so a later `command` field elsewhere in the payload would be rewritten instead; parse the JSON.

## Driver step clutter

Seen 2026-10-05 in `lyx-skills-and-stencils`: the LLM driver wraps every step as

```
exec </dev/null; export LYX_TRACE_ID=$(od -An -N8 -tx1 /dev/urandom | tr -d ' \n') && lyx shed step <run-id> 2>/dev/null > /tmp/tmp.XXXX/step-28.json; echo exit $?; cut -c1-1000 /tmp/tmp.XXXX/step-28.json
```

and each background job's completion notice repeats the whole line into the driver's context and pane.
`ly-drive` already says "Mint no `LYX_TRACE_ID`, create no `mktemp` step directory and add no redirects", since `lyx shed step` mints its own trace id and records each invocation under `.lyx`; the driver does it anyway.

Findings (hub, 2026-10-05):

- Every LLM driver since at least 2026-10-03 wraps its steps this way, in every run; `ly-drive` prescribed the wrapper until `083e992cf` (2026-09-30) and has forbidden it since, so the habit outlived the instruction.
- A likely motive: the skill says to read each step's trace, and the model mints its own id to find it, though the envelope already carries `trace_file`.
- Some drivers go further: `test-suite-measure`'s writes a `run.sh` through a heredoc into `/tmp`, the shape behind the stdin hang.
- The step stays a background job: Claude Code's Bash tool caps a foreground call at 2 minutes by default and 10 at most, and a step can block for an agent run of up to an hour.

Make the bare call the convenient one, so the model has nothing to wrap:

- `lyx shed step` prints a short envelope by default (outcome, producer, state, the next action), with the full envelope behind a flag or in its own record, so no `cut` or temp file is needed to read it.
- The driver stencil shows the one exact command to run, `lyx shed step <run-id>`, as a background job, and nothing else, and tells the driver where the trace is.

## Scope and coordination

Runs alongside `test-suite-prune-core` (owns `internal/shuttleengine`) and `test-suite-prune-rest` (owns `internal/shedcli` and the rest).
Touch only the tests that cover the changed behavior; the hub tells the prune runs to leave those alone.

Done when: no lyx-spawned Claude session carries the stdin hook, or the hook parses JSON if it must stay; `lyx shed step` prints a short envelope; the driver stencil shows the bare call.

entries.title: reed shows strands as zoom tabs and runs as session tabs
entries.brief: Stacked layout stays as VIEW; a strand button or Alt+arrows zooms one strand; runs as session tabs below; reed pins it at boot
entries.body:
reed runs one tmux session per run on the hub's one server, each with one window named `claude` whose panes are the run's strands, so the default status line shows nothing to switch between and a strand is hard to see on its own.

Chosen by the operator 2026-10-05 after a live demo on a separate server (`tmux -L lyxdemo`, session `run-c`): keep reed's current layout as the overview (driver on top at its fixed height, spawned strands below taking the rest, Selvage one line at the bottom), and show one strand at a time by zooming it.
Everything below is tmux's own options and bindings; reed pins them at server boot, like the `mouse` pin in `internal/reedengine/lifecycle.go`, so they survive a server restart.

- Line 1: a `VIEW` button lit when nothing is zoomed, then one button per strand, lit when that strand is zoomed; Selvage gets no button.
- Strand names come from a pane user option `@strand` that reed sets when it starts the strand (e.g. `driver`, `discussion-writer`), not from `pane_title`, which Claude Code overwrites with its own title; Selvage carries no `@strand`, which is what skips it.
- Line 2: one button per run (session), the current one lit, and the clock.
- Alt+z toggles between the overview and the zoomed strand; Alt+Up/Down moves to the previous/next strand and keeps the zoom; Alt+Left/Right switches run (operator, 2026-10-06).
- Pane borders carry the strand's title.

```
status 2
status-style bg=colour234,fg=white
status-format[0] "#[align=left]#{?window_zoomed_flag,#[bg=colour238#,fg=white],#[bg=cyan#,fg=black#,bold]} VIEW #[default]  #{P:#{?#{@strand},#[range=pane|#{pane_id}]#{?#{&&:#{window_zoomed_flag},#{pane_active}},#[bg=cyan#,fg=black#,bold],#[bg=colour236#,fg=white]} #{@strand} #[norange default] ,}}"
status-format[1] "#[align=left]#{S:#[range=session|#{session_id}]#{?#{==:#{session_name},#{client_session}},#[bg=yellow#,fg=black#,bold],#[bg=colour238#,fg=white]} #{session_name} #[norange default] }#[align=right]%H:%M "
pane-border-status top
pane-border-format " #{?pane_active,#[bold],}#{?#{@strand},#{@strand},selvage} "
bind -n M-z resize-pane -Z
bind -n M-Up select-pane -t :.- -Z
bind -n M-Down select-pane -t :.+ -Z
bind -n M-Left switch-client -p
bind -n M-Right switch-client -n
```

Status formats are one array: setting one index on a single session drops the global lines for that session, so set them globally only.

Open:

- Clicking a strand button while zoomed unzooms (tmux's default `MouseDown1Status` selects the pane); a root binding that re-zooms after the switch when the window was zoomed keeps it zoomed.
- Check that Claude Code does not need Alt+arrows or Alt+z in its input; tmux takes them first.
- VS Code's terminal swallows Alt+arrows and Alt+z, while Konsole passes them through; on 2026-10-06 the operator's user `keybindings.json` got one `workbench.action.terminal.sendSequence` entry per key (`\u001b[1;3A`–`D`, `\u001bz`, `when: terminalFocus`), which made them reach tmux.
  VS Code binds these keys itself (Alt+Left/Right focus the previous/next terminal in a group, Alt+z toggles word wrap), so the terminal never forwards them.
  `lyx ide` seeds these entries as part of its setup (operator, 2026-10-06); VS Code has no per-workspace keybindings, so they go in the user `keybindings.json` as a marked `// lyx:begin` … `// lyx:end` block that `lyx ide` rewrites, as mill does with its own block.
- `switch-client -n`/`-p` steps sessions in name order, but the `#{S:}` loop draws them in session-id order, so Alt+Left/Right jumped around the bar; on 2026-10-06 the bindings were replaced by a `run-shell` helper that steps through `list-sessions` sorted by session id.
  The operator wants spawn order (it matches how the runs sit on their desktop), so the bar keeps session-id order and switching follows it; the helper becomes a lyx verb such as `lyx reed switch --next|--prev` that the keys call.
  The binding passes `--socket '#{socket_path}' --client '#{client_name}'`, so the verb resolves nothing from a working directory: it lists the server's sessions, sorts them by session id and switches that client.
  Session ids are reassigned when the server restarts, so reed recreates the sessions in spawn order (the prime first, then each pair by its run's start time, read from the pair's own records), which keeps the order across a restart.
- Alt+Up/Down cycles every pane, Selvage included; skip it, e.g. by binding to a short reed-free tmux command that steps over panes without `@strand`.

Rejected in the demo: one window per strand (loses the overview, since a pane lives in one window only) and grouped sessions for a second view (hard to attach).

Related: `strand-colors` could tint the strand buttons and borders per role.

entries.title: A spawned role loads all its skills at once, not one turn per skill
entries.brief: lyx types each skill as its own slash-command turn, each ending in chatter; one typed message loads them all through the Skill tool in one turn
entries.body:
Since `70bf30ae8`, `claudeengine` types each of a role's skills as its own `/<name>` turn before the prompt pointer (`shuttleengine.Spec.Skills`).
Each turn is a full model turn that ends in a reply like "Loaded scribe:prose … What would you like to work on?", so a role with three skills spends three slow turns of chatter before it reads its task.
Seen 2026-10-05 on `ly:selfreport-issues-say-nothing:burler`; the operator: loading the skills is right, but all of them should load at once.

Claude Code treats only a message's leading `/<name>` as a command, so several skills cannot share one typed message.
Keep the guarantee that every skill is loaded, without a turn per skill:

- Chosen: one typed message asking the model to load every listed skill through the Skill tool in a single turn and reply only "ok".
  Loaded skills are registered as such, so Claude Code re-injects them after a compaction, and the instructions arrive as user input.
  lyx checks the transcript for each skill's load and retries a missing one.
- Rejected: inlining the skill bodies into the prompt file.
  It costs no turn, but the text arrives as a Read result rather than user input, and a compaction summarizes it away instead of re-injecting it, which matters for long-lived sessions such as the Webster master.

The orch watcher types its skills the same way at each cycle; the same fix applies there.


## From issue #394

Imported from [issue #394](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/394).

A skill the session does not know stalls a shuttle launch for the whole skill timeout, though a missing skill should be skipped at once.

Seen 2026-10-05 with `lyx orch start --handoff .scratch/handoff.md`: the `ly` plugin was read from a stale checkout without the `board` skill.
Shuttle typed `/ly:board`, Claude Code answered `Unknown command: /ly:board` in the pane, and the launch sat there until the skill timeout (600 s) skipped it.
To the operator, `lyx orch start` looked hung.

The orch docs (`internal/orchengine/doc.go`, "The reload sequence") already say a skill step is skipped "when the provider reports it unknown", but the provider does not see this answer:
`Unknown command` is printed by the slash-command parser, ends no turn and fires no Stop hook, so the step waits for a turn end that never comes.

Fix: detect the unknown-command answer (pane text after typing, or the transcript's local-command record) and skip the skill at once with a Warn naming it, in shuttle's launch skill loading and in the orch watcher's reload sequence alike.
A missing skill should never block a launch.

entries.title: Implementers hard-wrap comments and reviews re-find it every round
entries.brief: Bouncer re-finds hard-wrapped Go comments across rounds; catch it in the card gate or the implementer stencil
entries.body:
Webster implementers keep writing prose against `scribe:prose`'s line-break rule, and the Webster-Bouncer re-finds it round after round.
Seen in `board-labels-and-skills` (closed issues #372 and #373, filed by the removed Go anomaly reporter): `hard-wrapped-go-comments` stayed open in rounds 1, 2 and 4, and `independent-clauses-on-one-line` in rounds 2–4.
Each round spends a Burler fix and a Bouncer judgment on formatting the tooling could catch.

Options to settle in Discussion:

1. A guard test or `lyx` lint that flags fixed-column-wrapped comment blocks in changed Go files, run in the card gate, so the implementer fixes it before review.
2. The implementer stencil loads `scribe:prose` (or inlines its line-break rule), if it does not already.

Check first whether the stencils from `lyx-skills-and-stencils` already fixed it for new runs.

entries.title: Discussion stage has no sanctioned path to land a repository edit ahead of Plan
entries.brief: Discussion has no sanctioned path to commit a PATTERN edit ahead of Plan
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #385](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/385).

During the Discussion stage of a loom task, the parent (`ly:orch`) relayed an operator request to edit `PATTERN.md` and `pattern/` directly in the task worktree, so the review rounds would read the revised rules.

The Discussion launch prompt allows only the two discussion files and no git.
An uncommitted repository edit would leave the tree dirty for the `PATTERN-verified-tree` check.
It took an extra round trip to get the operator's explicit instruction and a named committer (the driver) before the edit could be made.

Discussion has no sanctioned path for "land this invariant now, ahead of Plan".
If this should be supported, the Discussion launch prompt or the parent-review flow needs a carve-out that names who commits such an edit, instead of leaving it to an ad-hoc message exchange.

Provenance: task `test-writing-rules`, note `Discussion-Write.md`.

entries.title: The orch resumes runs without commands that take over the operator's terminal
entries.brief: lyx loom start from the orch switches the operator's tmux client; the orch needs a side-effect-free resume verb
entries.body:
Seen 2026-10-06: the prime's reed window jumped to other sessions "by itself" while the operator watched the orch.
The cause was the orch's own `lyx loom start` calls in task worktrees: the orch runs inside reed's tmux, so `$TMUX` is set, and `lyx loom start` without `--no-attach` runs `tmux switch-client` onto the task's session (`internal/loomcli/start.go`), taking the operator's terminal with it.
`lyx orch start` does the same without `--no-attach` (`internal/orchcli/handover.go`).

The orch role (`contracts/stencils/orch/orch-template-role.md`) tells the orch to resume a halted child with `lyx loom start`, an operator verb whose job includes handing over the terminal.
In practice the call also did not move the runs: a live driver resumed only once the orch messaged it.

## Direction

- The orch resumes a child through a verb with no interactive side effect: a resume verb that only records the decision and wakes the run's driver (or batten), never spawning or attaching anything.
  The role stencil names that verb and never `lyx loom start`.
- `lyx loom start` and `lyx orch start` never switch the tmux client when called from an agent (`LYX_STRAND_NAME` set), whatever the flags; the terminal handoff is for an operator's shell only.

The bug half (no tmux switch-client from an agent) is in task `bugfix-sessions`; this note keeps the orch resume verb.

Operator decision 2026-10-06: start verbs never attach a terminal for any caller; attaching is only `lyx reed attach` (implemented in `bugfix-sessions`).

entries.title: One prompt notice channel to the orch: batten, event-driven, timestamped
entries.brief: Driver and batten both report every halt, and batten's 30 s poll makes its notices late and stale
entries.body:
Seen 2026-10-06: the orch gets two messages for every halt, and the batten one is often stale.

- The driver messages the orch at once with its stop report.
- Batten's Run-Shed row polls the child only every `poll_interval_s: 30` (`contracts/recipes/batten-recipe.yaml`), so its `[batten notice]` lags up to half a minute.
- The notice is typed into the orch pane and read only when the orch's current turn ends; by then the orch has often resumed the run, and the notice reports a state that no longer holds (twice on 2026-10-06: "paused" and "awaiting" for runs already running again).

## Direction

- One channel per event: batten owns state changes (blocked, paused, awaiting PR-Gate, done) and its notice carries the drive report path; the driver messages the orch only with a question it cannot settle itself, never with "the run stopped".
  Parent-review requests and escalation briefs keep coming from the producer session.
- The notice is event-driven, not polled: batten wakes on the child's status-file change (or polls at a few seconds), since the orch relies on it as its only wake-up.
- Each notice carries the time the state held and the child's history length, so a stale notice is recognisable without a status call.

Related notes: `orch-owns-the-loop` (detached batten start, a lyx watch) and `runs-overview` (notices shortened, the event log in its own window).

entries.title: Bugfix: session lifecycle, notices and run halts
entries.brief: Bugfix only: prompt delivery, stale producer sessions, false crash notes, watcher restart, Burler YAML repair, no client switch from agents
entries.body:
Bugfix only (operator, 2026-10-06): fix what each section below reports, with a regression test per fix that drives the real CLI wiring, not only fakes.
No new verbs, config keys or features; a reviewer treats any extension as a scope finding.
The board adds more bug sections here until the task starts.

Scope limits: from `orch-resume-without-attach`, only the terminal handoff, and the orch resume verb is not part of this task.
Operator decision 2026-10-06: `lyx loom start` and `lyx orch start` never attach or switch a tmux client, for any caller; attaching to reed is only `lyx reed attach`.
The attach code path and the `--no-attach` flag go (the flag may stay as an accepted no-op for one release if callers pass it); docs and stencils that mention the handoff follow.

## producer-session-handoff

Imported from [issue #395](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/395).

reed's `SendText` sometimes types a prompt into a Claude Code pane without submitting it, and the session sits with the text in its input box until someone presses Enter.

Seen 2026-10-05 at `lyx orch start --handoff …`: the launch pointer (`Read …/prompt.md in full first; …`, two wrapped lines) stayed unsent; the operator pressed Enter by hand.
The short skill loads before it (`/scribe:prose`, `/ly:board`) were submitted.

`SendText` (`internal/reedengine/io.go`) runs `send-keys -l <text>` and then `send-keys Enter` back to back.
Claude Code's input treats a fast burst of characters as a paste, and an Enter that arrives inside the burst becomes part of it instead of a submit.
The longer the text and the busier the machine, the likelier the race.

Fix options:

1. Send the text as a bracketed paste (`load-buffer` + `paste-buffer -p`), so the TUI knows where the paste ends, then Enter.
2. After Enter, confirm the input box emptied (capture the pane, or wait for the transcript's user record) and resend Enter once if not.

Option 2 also covers other causes of a lost Enter; the two combine.
Every typed delivery (shuttle launch pointers and skill loads, orch watcher reloads, batten notices, `SendMessage`-style relays through reed) goes through this path.


### From issue #399

Imported from [issue #399](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/399).

`reflectHalt` (`internal/loomcli/halt.go`) writes `loom-halt.md` and at once runs `reflectFriction(false)`, which spawns a reflection agent session on every halt.
That includes a `blocked` halt classified `escalation-to-human`, where the producer's own session is still live and holds the open question.

Seen 2026-10-06 on `test-suite-prune-core`: Plan-Write halted `blocked` with "agent is asking a question".
While the plan session stood waiting, the run spawned a friction-reflection session; its report said only "an escalation, a process signal and not a lyx defect".
To the operator this looked like the run moving on while its producer hung.

Expected: an `escalation-to-human` halt writes the halt note but spawns no reflection.
The terminal Friction-Reflect row reads the note anyway.


### From issue #400

Imported from [issue #400](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/400).

When a halted run is moved back to a producer with `lyx loom goto --to <producer>` and resumed, the producer spawns a fresh session (`ly:<slug>:plan-2`) but leaves the halted attempt's session (`ly:<slug>:plan`) alive.
Both sessions then hold the same producer's instructions, and anything that wakes the old one (an operator message, a submitted input) puts two agents on the same output files.

Seen 2026-10-06 on `test-suite-prune-core`: Plan-Write halted `blocked` because its prompt pointer was never submitted (#395) and a hub message ended a turn.
After `goto --to Plan-Write` and a re-step, `plan-2` started while `plan` still held the unsubmitted pointer; submitting it ran two plan writers at once until `plan` was removed with `lyx reed remove`.

Expected: re-invoking a producer after a halt removes that producer's previous strand before spawning the new one, or reattaches to it, never both alive.

### Webster recovery strand left behind (2026-10-06)

A failed `recover-batch` leaves its `ly:<slug>:recovery` strand alive and idle after reporting.
On `skills-in-one-turn` it stayed beside the new Webster Master after a `webster reset --to start` and `goto --to Webster`, until removed by hand.
The same rule applies: a finished or superseded session is removed, never left beside its successor.

## false-crash-resume

Imported from [issue #396](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/396).

### What happened

`lyx shed step` (the `step` verb) wrote a `loom-crash-resume` note ("loom resumed after a suspected driver crash at Webster-Bouncer") with `state: running`, `current_producer: Webster-Bouncer`.
The run history's last entry was `Webster / done`, recorded about six seconds before the step started.
The step then ran normally: a bouncer-seed shuttle run finished with `outcome=done`, and `shed: step done` reported `outcome=stuck next=Webster-Burler`.
Nothing in the trace shows a crash; the run was advancing from one producer to the next.

### Why it is abnormal

A crash-resume note is meant to mark a run that was last stopped without a clean handoff.
Here the previous producer completed and the next one had not yet started, so the note is most likely a false positive from the gap between two producers (the next row marked current, its run not yet begun).
The note also gives no reason for the "suspected" crash, so the operator cannot tell whether it is real.

### What to do

Check what `lyx shed step` / `lyx loom step` uses to decide that the previous driver crashed, and whether a run that is `running` with a freshly completed previous row should count.
Include the evidence (heartbeat, pid or lock state) in the note so a real crash and a false positive can be told apart.

Provenance: task `test-suite-measure`; notes: `loom-crash-resume.md`.


### From issue #392

Imported from [issue #392](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/392).

### What happened

`lyx shed step` wrote a `loom-crash-resume` friction note ("loom resumed after a suspected driver crash at Webster-Bouncer") for a run that had not crashed.

- The run's last history entry was `Webster / done`, recorded six seconds before the flagged step began.
- A `lyx board sync` ran in that gap, as it does after a finished producer.
- The flagged step itself ran normally: `shuttle: run started` then `run finished outcome=done`, then `shed: step done producer=Webster-Bouncer outcome=stuck state=running next=Webster-Burler`.
- The status was `state: running` with `current_producer: Webster-Bouncer`, which is the ordinary state between two steps.

### Why it is abnormal

A clean handoff between two steps was classified as "last stopped without a clean handoff".
The note sends the reader looking for a driver crash that did not occur.

Two smaller defects in the same note:

- It reports `history_entries: 14` but lists only five history lines, with no marker that the list is truncated.
- Its history ends at `Webster / done` and omits the later entries, so it cannot be used to tell whether the stop was clean.

### What to do

- Check the crash-detection condition in the `lyx shed step` / `lyx loom step` entry path: a run whose last producer finished `done` and whose next producer has not started should not count as crashed.
- State in the note when the history list is truncated, or list all entries.

### Provenance

Task slug `board-config-per-worktree`; note file `loom-crash-resume.md`.

## orch-watcher-stale-reload

Imported from [issue #390](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/390).

On 2026-10-05 the hub restarted a stale `lyx orch watch` (it ran a binary from 2026-10-02) with `lyx orch start --no-attach`, keeping the live orch session.
The new watcher at once ran the post-compaction reload: it typed `/scribe:prose`, `/scribe:conversation` and the role-file pointer into a session that had been working normally for hours.

The compaction it reacted to was a manual `/compact` hours before the restart.
On its first tick the watcher reads the events from the persisted cursor (`phase_events_offset`, last advanced on 2026-10-04 by the old watcher), finds that compaction through `CompactedSince`, and starts `startAutoReload` as if it had just happened.

Expected:

- A reload follows only a compaction newer than the session's last completed turn; a compaction followed by later turns needs none.
- The reload types only what a compaction loses. Claude Code re-injects the skills a session has invoked after a compaction, so typing them again is a duplicate; the role file, read through a pointer, is what is lost.


### From issue #393

Imported from [issue #393](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/393).

The orch session cannot load `ly:board`, though the role procedure (`.lyx/orch/role.md`) and the orch watcher's reload both point to it.

Seen 2026-10-05 in the hub's orch session, after deploying `c140db21a` with `update-plugins.sh`:

- `~/.claude/plugins/cache/loomyard/ly/1.0.0/skills/board/SKILL.md` exists, and the prime's `.claude/settings.json` enables `ly@loomyard`.
- The Skill tool answers `Unknown skill: ly:board`, both before and after the watcher's role reload.
- The session's Claude Code process started on 2026-10-03, and `lyx orch` keeps it alive across context cycles through `/compact` and a typed reload.

Claude Code reads the skill list when the process starts.
A skill added or renamed by a later deploy stays unknown to a long-lived session, and so does every procedure that names it.

Possible fixes:

1. A context cycle, or the first cycle after a deploy, restarts the Claude Code process (`claude --resume` or a fresh session with the orch note) instead of compacting in place.
2. `update-plugins.sh` tells the running orch that skills changed, and the watcher schedules a restart.
3. The reload message checks that each skill it names loads, and reports a missing one to the operator instead of failing silently in the session.

### Restart race (2026-10-06)

`kill <pid of lyx orch watch>` followed at once by `lyx orch start --no-attach` answered `attach-only` and spawned no watcher, since the old watcher still read as live.
A second `lyx orch start --no-attach` a moment later spawned it.
`start` should wait for a watcher it sees dying, or the restart needs its own verb.

## burler-yaml-frontmatter-repair

Imported from [issue #386](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/386).

A loom run halted as `failed` at the `Discussion-Burler` producer (burler adapter in `internal/shedadapters`).

Halt output:

```
shedadapters: Discussion-Burler (burler): round 3 attempt 3: run: burler: round reached done but its review file is invalid: burler: review file frontmatter is not valid YAML: yaml: line 12: did not find expected key (a summary containing a " character must be ONE double-quoted string covering the whole value, not a quoted fragment followed by trailing prose)
```

The reviewer agent wrote a review file whose frontmatter summary contained a quoted fragment followed by trailing prose, which is invalid YAML.
The error text already states the rule, yet the run still failed at round 3 attempt 3 with history_entries 8.
Possible fixes: have the burler round prompt show the quoting rule up front, feed the parse error back to the reviewer for a repair turn, or have the frontmatter reader tolerate or normalise an unquoted summary.

Provenance: task `test-suite-measure`, from note `loom-halt.md`.

## orch-resume-without-attach

Seen 2026-10-06: the prime's reed window jumped to other sessions "by itself" while the operator watched the orch.
The cause was the orch's own `lyx loom start` calls in task worktrees: the orch runs inside reed's tmux, so `$TMUX` is set, and `lyx loom start` without `--no-attach` runs `tmux switch-client` onto the task's session (`internal/loomcli/start.go`), taking the operator's terminal with it.
`lyx orch start` does the same without `--no-attach` (`internal/orchcli/handover.go`).

The orch role (`contracts/stencils/orch/orch-template-role.md`) tells the orch to resume a halted child with `lyx loom start`, an operator verb whose job includes handing over the terminal.
In practice the call also did not move the runs: a live driver resumed only once the orch messaged it.

### Direction

- The orch resumes a child through a verb with no interactive side effect: a resume verb that only records the decision and wakes the run's driver (or batten), never spawning or attaching anything.
  The role stencil names that verb and never `lyx loom start`.
- `lyx loom start` and `lyx orch start` never switch the tmux client when called from an agent (`LYX_STRAND_NAME` set), whatever the flags; the terminal handoff is for an operator's shell only.

entries.title: Bugfix: Webster and plan validity
entries.brief: Bugfix only: Plan-Gate refuses backward dependencies, Delete of a gone target, background-shell wait, slow batch validation
entries.body:
Bugfix only (operator, 2026-10-06): fix what each section below reports, with a regression test per fix that drives the real CLI wiring, not only fakes.
No new verbs, config keys or features; a reviewer treats any extension as a scope finding.
The board adds more bug sections here until the task starts.

Scope limits: from `webster-delete-ordering`, only the Plan-Gate refusal of backward dependencies and cycles; Webster dropping its own sequencing is not part of this task.

## webster-delete-already-gone

Seen 2026-10-03 in the `verify-publish-hardening` run, after 12 batches.
Batch 15 (card 15, `webster-verify-gate`) deleted `internal/websterengine/integration_test.go`, even though card 15 does not list it.
Card 17 lists the file under **Delete:**, so batch 16's `begin-batch` refused with `plan_drifted`: the path does not exist on disk and is not a Create target or Rename destination of any card.
The run blocked until the plan was edited by hand and rebaselined.

A Delete target that is already gone is the state the card wants, so it should not block the run.
Options:
- `begin-batch` accepts a missing **Delete:** path when an earlier batch's commit deleted it, and notes it in the batch record.
- The per-card check flags a batch that deletes a file outside its card, at the batch where it happens rather than at a later card.


From GitHub #352 (intake 2026-10-04).

## webster-delete-ordering

### Rule (operator, 2026-10-06)

A valid plan is executable strictly in card-number order: implementing card 1, then 2, then 3 and so on always works.
A card never depends on anything a later card does.
Webster follows that order as written and never sorts cards.

This reverses `contracts/specs/loom-plan-spec.md`, which today calls the card list a DAG of intent "not itself an execution order" and lets the executor derive the order (`websterengine.SequenceBatches`, `deriveEdges` in `internal/websterengine/sequence.go`).

### What changes

- **Plan-Gate refuses a backward dependency.** A card whose `Uses:` names a target of a later card, a card that deletes a symbol still referenced from a member a later card edits, and any derived dependency cycle are blocking findings, so an invalid plan never reaches Webster.
- **Webster drops its own ordering.** Batches run in card-number order; `SequenceBatches` and its cycle condensation go, or reduce to an assertion that the plan already satisfies every edge.
- **The plan spec and the plan template** state the rule to the plan writer and the plan reviewer.

### Sightings

- 2026-10-03, `pair-lifecycle` (GitHub #350): card 12 deleted `fabricengine.Topology.RemovePairBranch`, `PairBranchResult` and `PairSiblingRemnant` and ran before card 11, which removed their only production caller in `internal/battencli/wire.go`; the batch failed and the run blocked at Webster.
- 2026-10-06, `skills-in-one-turn`: card 2's `Uses:` named `internal/shuttleengine#Runner.skillLoader`, which card 4 edits, a backward dependency; cards 2 and 4 also shared test-file targets.
  `SequenceBatches` condensed the cycle {2, 4} and ran 01, 02, 04, 03, so card 4 deleted `SkillLoader.SkillLoadSequence`, `SkillUnknown` and `Runner.LoadSkill` before card 3 moved `internal/orchengine` and `internal/orchcli` off them.
  The cycle surfaced only as an unread `Cycle` warning.
  `webster rebaseline` refused the fix because batch 4 had begun, so the run needed `webster reset --to start`, an archived `state.json` and a goto, redoing two finished batches.

## webster-background-shell-wait

Imported from [issue #397](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/397).

### What happened

`lyx webster` wrote a `webster-background-shell` note titled "Master's wait counted a turn end past a background shell".
It lists a background shell, a polling `until grep -q '^done$' <log>; do sleep 5; done` loop, that had run past `background_shell_wait_min` (10 minutes) while Master's turn end was being judged.
The note says the shell may still be running in the session.

### Why it is abnormal

The note records that Master's turn end was counted although a background shell was still alive past the wait limit.
It is unclear whether the turn end should have been held until the shell finished, or whether the shell should have been stopped.
A shell left running across a turn end can outlive its purpose or race with the next step, and the note gives the operator no outcome: whether the shell was killed, whether the wait gave up, and what the run did next.

### What to do

Decide the intended behavior when `background_shell_wait_min` elapses with a shell still running: keep waiting, kill the shell, or escalate.
Make the note state which of these happened.

Provenance: task `test-suite-measure`; notes: `webster-background-shell.md`.

## webster-batch-validation-speed

Seen on `test-suite-change-amplification` (2026-10-03), a 45-card plan that the Batchifier split into one card per batch.

### Measured

- `lyx webster validate` on that plan takes 64 s of wall time at 100 % of one core, with no child processes: the time is spent in-process, single-threaded.
- `begin-batch` runs `planglyph.ValidateDispatch` over the whole plan before every batch (`internal/websterengine/beginbatch.go:303`), so each batch pays roughly that cost again.
- The gap from one batch's report to the next batch's spawn was 143 s, 72 s and 81 s for the first three batches, while the forks themselves took 1–2 min each.
  Over 45 batches that is on the order of 50 minutes of setup.

### Cause

Not loomyard's own code: `quarry.Repo.Resolve` re-parses every file in a target's directory for each file target (Knatte18/quarry#34).

### Per-batch validation stays (operator)

Validating before every batch is deliberate.
A fork may drift from the plan when it finds something the plan missed, and the plan changes with it; the per-batch check is what notices.
It is also the base for running forks in parallel later: glyphs, quarry and the validator maintain, at every batch, a DAG that decides which cards and batches can run concurrently.

### Want

- quarry#34 fixed and the quarry dependency bumped, so one validation of a plan this size takes seconds.
- If that is not enough, make the per-batch validation incremental: re-resolve only the targets in files the last batch's delta touched, plus the cards that reference them, and reuse the rest from the previous batch.
- Drop `begin-batch`'s per-batch model assertion (operator): the fork inherits Merriam's model, so `begin-batch` has no model to check.

### Related

The one-card-per-batch split makes the per-batch cost dominate; whether the Batchifier should group cards more is a separate question.


From GitHub #345 (intake 2026-10-04).


## From issue #401

Imported from [issue #401](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/401).

## What happened

A loom run passed Plan-Write, Plan-Bouncer and Batchifier with a batch order in which batch 04 (a delete-only card) ran before batch 03.
Batch 04 deletes symbols that batch 03 still uses, so the delete cannot be done without doing batch 03's work.
The agent assigned to batch 04 noticed this, stopped without editing anything and wrote a friction note.
`lyx webster record-batch 04` then refused with `batch_failed` and ten `delete-not-done/...[blocking]` findings ("Delete target ... still resolves").
The refusal output ends with `way forward: lyx webster recover-batch 04`.
`lyx webster recover-batch 04` refused with the same ten findings and the same `way forward: lyx webster recover-batch 04`.
The run halted `blocked` at Webster with anomaly `escalation-to-human` (history ends `Webster / stuck`).

## Why it is abnormal

- The plan and batch order carried a dependency inversion that neither Plan-Bouncer nor Batchifier caught, although the card's own text referred to the other card as already done.
  Batch ordering has no dependency check, or it ignores the dependency the plan states.
- The refusal's `way forward` points at a verb that cannot succeed.
  `recover-batch` re-runs the same `delete-not-done` check against an unchanged tree, so following the hint loops.
  The real cause (batch order) is not named in the refusal.

## What to do

- Have Plan-Bouncer or Batchifier reject or reorder a batch whose delete targets are still referenced by a later batch, or that depends on a batch ordered after it.
- When `delete-not-done` is blocking and a later batch still references the target, say so in the refusal, and do not suggest `recover-batch` as the way forward when nothing has changed since the failure.

Provenance: task `skills-in-one-turn`; notes `04-drop-per-skill-load.md`, `loom-halt.md`, `webster-refusal-record-batch.md`, `webster-refusal-recover-batch.md`.


## From issue #402

Imported from [issue #402](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/402).

What happened:
In one loom run, for three separate batches, `lyx webster begin-batch <n>` was refused because a report for the batch already existed under `_lyx/webster/reports/`.
The refusal text says a report left behind by a crashed session is consumed by `lyx webster record-batch <n>`.
`lyx webster record-batch <n>` was then refused for the same batch: "record-batch called with no begin-batch record for this batch".
It archived the report with a timestamp suffix and told the caller to run `lyx webster begin-batch <nn>` again.

Why it is abnormal:
The two verbs' guidance points at each other.
begin-batch says "record the existing report", and record-batch says "no begin-batch record exists, begin again".
Only the archive side effect of the failed record-batch breaks the loop, which makes the recovery path indirect and costs two refused calls per batch.
It happened for every batch in the run, so it looks like a systematic ordering problem (a report being present before begin-batch recorded its start), not a one-off crash.

What to do:
Find what writes the batch report before the begin-batch record exists.
Make begin-batch either adopt or archive a report that has no begin-batch record, so the refusal message names a path that works the first time.
The webster-refusal notes also don't say which of the two states the caller was in, so the refusal could include it.

Provenance: task skills-in-one-turn; notes webster-refusal-begin-batch.md, webster-refusal-begin-batch-2.md, webster-refusal-begin-batch-3.md, webster-refusal-record-batch.md, webster-refusal-record-batch-2.md, webster-refusal-record-batch-3.md.


## From issue #403

Imported from [issue #403](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/403).

What happened:
`lyx webster rebaseline --card=04` was refused: "the edited plan changes the cards of a batch this run already begun: batch 4 card ... changed since it was begun".
The only way forward offered was to restore the cards in the plan, or `lyx webster reset --to start` followed by `lyx webster run --fresh`.

Why it is abnormal:
The `--card` flag implies a targeted rebaseline of one card.
The refusal then only allows discarding the whole run's progress, which is disproportionate for a one-card edit and is not a path an agent can take on its own mid-run.

What to do:
Either let rebaseline accept an intentional edit to a begun card when `--card` names it (resetting only that batch), or have the refusal explain why `--card` cannot do so and offer a narrower way forward such as `lyx webster recover-batch`.

Provenance: task skills-in-one-turn; note webster-refusal-rebaseline.md.


## From issue #404

Imported from [issue #404](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/404).

What happened:
The loom run halted `blocked` at the Publish producer with anomaly `escalation-to-human` and reason "push rejected by the remote".
The trace shows `landingshed: producer stuck` with error "gitrepo: push rejected (remote diverged)", right after "post-merge verify skipped because the tree is already verified".
The run's earlier steps (Webster review, Describe) were all done.
The step ended with `state=blocked next=Publish`.

Why it is abnormal:
A diverged remote at push time is a routine race when other runs or pushes land on the parent branch.
Halting for a human at the last step of a finished run throws away no work but needs manual intervention for a condition lyx could handle.
It is unclear from the halt note whether Publish re-fetched and re-integrated before giving up.

What to do:
Check whether landingshed's Publish refetches, re-integrates and re-verifies once on a diverged push before escalating.
If it does not, add a bounded retry, and make the halt note say what Publish tried and what the operator should run to resume.

Provenance: task skills-in-one-turn; note loom-halt.md.

entries.title: Bugfix: fabric and config propagation
entries.brief: Bugfix only: a weft without .weft/ drops LYX_PARENT, task config changes never reach the parent, and fabric ignores existing origin branches when it builds a pair
entries.body:
Bugfix only (operator, 2026-10-06): fix what each section below reports, with a regression test per fix that drives the real CLI wiring, not only fakes.
No new verbs, config keys or features; a reviewer treats any extension as a scope finding.
The board adds more bug sections here until the task starts.
One exception, by operator decision (2026-10-06): `fabric-add-adopt-remote` below is in scope whole, including `lyx fabric add` adopting existing origin branches.

## weft-lock-dir-drops-parent

### Bug

A strand launched in a pair whose weft worktree lacks the untracked `.weft/` lock directory gets no `LYX_PARENT`, silently.
`hubgeom.ResolveParent` reads the pair's origin record through `fabricengine.ReadOriginFor`, which requires both `_lyx/fabric/origin.json` and `.weft/`, and answers "no record" when either is missing.
`ResolveParent` then returns no parent, `hubgeom.reedGeometry` exports none, and nothing warns.

### Seen 2026-10-05

After moving `loom-bouncer-rounds` from another machine, its weft worktree was recreated by `lyx fabric reconcile` from the existing branch, which does not create `.weft/` (`lyx fabric add` does).
The driver, launched at 15:36:00, had no `LYX_PARENT`; `.weft/` appeared at 15:36:19 with the first weft write, and the Burler launched at 15:58 carries `LYX_PARENT='ly:orch'`.
The driver therefore could not reach its parent orchestrator.

### Fix

- Every path that creates or recreates a weft worktree creates `.weft/` (`reconcile`'s `weft_recreated` path at least).
- A present origin record with a missing lock directory is an error or a warning naming the gap, never a silent "no parent".

## config-reaches-parent

Seen 2026-10-04 twice: `pattern-init` first planned to keep PATTERN under `_lyx/` and needed a landing carry (dropped by moving PATTERN to warp), and `board-model`'s parent review found its D13 label list written into the pair's `_lyx/config/board.yaml`, which never reaches the parent.
Live config lives in weft, and a task's weft branch dies at landing, so any config change a task makes is lost unless the hub re-applies it by hand on main's weft.
Idea: either a landing step that carries `_lyx/config/` changes into the parent's weft (with a conflict stop), or task-made config changes declared in the PR description and applied by the hub as a checked step.

## fabric-add-adopt-remote

### Problem

Moving a running task to another machine needs a pair built from the task's existing warp and weft branches on origin.
Fabric handles an existing warp: `lyx fabric reconcile` adopts a warp worktree created outside lyx.
Finding the existing weft is the gap: `reconcile`, `checkout` and `add` probe only the local `refs/heads/<slug>-weft` (`weftBranchExists`).
When that ref is absent, `reconcile` forks a fresh dormant weft from the weft HEAD (`createDormantWeftForRawWarp`) and never looks at `origin/<slug>-weft`, so the run records and status are silently lost and the next push collides with origin.
Only `clone` adopts a weft branch from origin, and only for the prime.

### Workaround used on 2026-10-05

```
git -C <hub>/<repo>-weft branch --track <slug>-weft origin/<slug>-weft
git worktree add --track -b <slug> ../<slug> origin/<slug>
lyx fabric reconcile
```

With the local tracking weft branch in place, `reconcile` takes its `weft_recreated` path and wires junctions, portal and launchers.
`lyx batten run <slug>` from prime then resumed both the outer and the inner run, and the inner loom run continued from its producer row with a fresh agent.

The adopted pair's strands also lost their parent until the first weft write: see `weft-lock-dir-drops-parent` above.

### Proposal

When a branch exists on origin, fabric fetches it and checks it out as a tracking branch; it never creates a new local branch in its place.
`lyx fabric add <slug>` fetches `origin/<slug>` and `origin/<slug>-weft` when they exist, instead of refusing the warp branch as a diverged leftover.
Every other path that resolves a pair's weft branch (`reconcile`, `checkout`) checks `origin/<slug>-weft` the same way before forking a new one, as `clone` does.

entries.title: Shortcut commands built into lyx from one committed file
entries.brief: An embedded shortcut file, git-alias style: attach for reed attach, and one shortcut that starts the orch and attaches in the prime
entries.body:
Idea (operator, 2026-10-06): top-level shortcuts for the lyx commands the operator types most, declared in one simple file in this repo rather than as Go commands.

Examples:

- `attach` expands to `reed attach`.
- One shortcut for the prime runs `orch start`, then `reed attach`; the orch always runs in the prime.
  Name open: `spawn` was floated; `up` would read like `reed up`.
  It fits the decision recorded in task `bugfix-sessions` that start verbs never attach: the shortcut is where both happen, by naming `reed attach` explicitly.

## Shape (operator, 2026-10-06)

- The shortcuts are part of the deployed `lyx` binary, the same on every hub and repo: a committed file in the loomyard repo, embedded at build time (`go:embed`), never runtime config.
  No hub, repo or user can add or change one; changing a shortcut is a commit here and a deploy.
- The file maps a shortcut name to one lyx argv, or to a list of argvs run in order that stops at the first failure.
  Only lyx commands, never a shell string.
- At root construction lyx adds one cobra command per shortcut, in its own help group, whose `Short` names the expansion; running it re-dispatches the expanded args through the same root, so flags, envelopes and exit codes are the real command's.
  Extra args after the shortcut append to the last argv.
- A test fails when a shortcut names an existing command or another shortcut, or expands to a command that does not exist, so a broken file never builds into a binary that passes CI.

## Open

- Whether a shortcut may carry flags of its own or only append args.

More shortcuts get added here as the operator notices them.
Related notes: `ide-prime-setup` (a VS Code task that starts the orch) and `ide-reopen-prime` (reopen the prime window with one command).

entries.title: Spawned agents edit files with scripts; the no-script rule never reaches them
entries.body:
Seen 2026-10-06 in `test-suite-prune-core`, batch 10's recovery strand: the agent edited `internal/websterengine/beginbatch_test.go` with an inline `python3 - <<'EOF'` script, and the edit left an unused `strconv` import that vet caught.

The rule "change files only with Edit or Write, never with a script that rewrites them (sed, awk, perl, python, node)" lives in `scribe:conversation`, a chat skill.
Spawned implementer, recovery and fixer roles load `scribe:prose`, `scribe:code-quality` and `scribe:testing`, so they never see it.

Fix direction: state the rule where every file-editing role reads it: the implementer and recovery stencils under `contracts/stencils/webster/`, the Burler fixer and Rework stencils, or one shared prefix they all compose.

entries.title: Shuttle: a turn end without output holds the run instead of ending it
entries.brief: An asking stop ends the run while the agent lives on, so an answer is lost and a resume spawns a second agent; hold the run and wait on the same agent instead.
entries.body:
## Problem

A turn end without every output file present ends a shuttle run as `asking`, a terminal outcome, while the agent stays alive in its pane.
Nothing waits on that agent any more:
an answer sent into its session makes it work on, unobserved,
and resuming the producer starts a second agent on the same outputs.

Seen 2026-10-06 in `bugfix-sessions` Plan-Write: the plan agent asked a question, ly:orch answered it in the session, the driver resumed the step, and shuttle spawned `plan-2` beside the still-working first agent; ly:orch removed the first one, losing the work done after the answer.

The same rule makes any message to a working agent dangerous: the agent replies, its turn ends without its outputs, and the run halts as `asking`.

## Proposal

A turn end without output never ends a run.

- A turn end with every output file present is done, as today.
- A dead agent and a timeout end the run, as today.
- A turn end without the outputs holds the run with the agent alive: shuttle notifies the parent once that the agent is waiting, and keeps waiting on the same agent.
- An answer to the agent, from the parent, a driver or the operator, is a new turn in the same session; shuttle keeps waiting.
- Resuming the producer attaches to the held run instead of starting a new agent.
- Every message sent to a working agent carries a fixed tail, "Answer briefly, then continue your task", so it replies and works on by itself; senders add it today, and `creel` adds it once it lands.

The cost: a stop no longer halts the run at once; the parent's notice and the run's timeout are the only signals.

## Related

`bugfix-sessions` card 5 removes a live agent of the same outputs before a fresh run, which ends the duplicate but not the lost answer.
The `creel` note owns message delivery and would add the tail.


## From issue #407

Imported from [issue #407](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/407).

lyx wrote a note, "Master's wait counted a turn end past a background shell", stating that background shells ran past `background_shell_wait_min` (10 minutes) while Master's turn end was being judged, and may still be running in the session.
The shell was a multi-step measurement script launched by Master and still unfinished when the turn end was classified.

This is abnormal because the turn end was judged, and the wait counted, while work Master had started was unfinished.
The note itself says the shell may still be running, so lyx does not know whether the turn end was genuine or whether Master was merely waiting on its own background job.
That risks a premature stuck or escalation verdict (this run's Webster segment subsequently went stuck several times and halted with an escalation-to-human anomaly).

Suggested fix: when a background shell exceeds `background_shell_wait_min`, have lyx either keep waiting on it or report its final state, rather than only noting that it may still be running.

Provenance: task `test-suite-prune-core`; notes `webster-background-shell.md`, `loom-halt.md`.

entries.title: Run tabs overflow a narrow terminal once several runs are open
entries.brief: The status line row of run tabs prints full session names, so with five runs the rightmost fall off a narrow terminal unseen
entries.body:
## Seen 2026-10-06

With five runs and the prime open, the session row of the status line (the run tabs from `reed-status-tabs`) is wider than a narrow terminal, and the rightmost runs fall off the edge with no sign that they exist.
The row prints every session's full name with padding, and run slugs such as `test-suite-prune-core` are long.

## Options

1. Current session full, others truncated, overflow scrolls (recommended): the session the client is in shows its full name, every other session is cut to about 12 characters (`#{=12:session_name}`), and the row uses tmux's list mode (`list=on`, `list=focus`, left and right markers), so a row that still overflows scrolls with `<` and `>` markers and keeps the current session visible.
2. Index only for other sessions, the current one by full name: the most compact, but the operator has to remember which number is which run.
3. List-mode scrolling alone, full names kept: the least change, with the fewest sessions visible at once.
4. Wrap the session row onto further status lines: costs terminal height, and tmux has no automatic wrap, so reed would compute the split itself.

The run tabs' design is in the note `reed-status-tabs`.

entries.title: reed: stray strands after a crash
entries.brief: After a crash, folder-open adds a bare claude above a dormant orch, and reed resume revives strands whose work is done
entries.body:
Two reed bugs seen on 2026-10-06 when the machine crashed and the runs were brought back.

## Bare claude strand above a dormant orch (issue #408)

After a machine crash, opening the hub prime in VS Code left an empty `ly:claude` strand in the prime's reed session, with the `ly:orch` strand stacked below it.

Cause: the folder-open task chain written by `internal/vscode/config.go` runs `lyx reed add --if-absent --unless-name orch --name claude`.
`--unless-name` skips the add only while the orch strand is live (`AddStrandUnless`, `internal/reedengine/strand.go`).
After a reboot the orch strand is persisted but dormant, so the check passes, a bare `claude` strand is added, and the orch is resumed into the same session afterwards.

Expected: a prime whose reed state holds an orch strand, live or dormant, gets no bare `claude` strand on folder-open.
Possible fixes: let `--unless-name` also match a persisted dormant strand, or have the folder-open chain run `lyx reed resume` before the add.

## Resume revives strands whose work is done (issue #409)

After a machine crash, `lyx reed resume` in the `test-suite-prune-core` pair recreated two strands: the driver and `ly:test-suite-prune-core:burler`.
The burler's round had finished before the crash (verdict written and committed), and the run had moved on.
When the driver re-ran its shed step, the next producer spawned its own strand (`describe`), so the pair showed a dead-weight burler pane beside the live one.

Cause: a strand stays persisted in reed's state after the work it was spawned for is done, since only the shuttle wait that would tear it down died with the crash; `resume` replays every persisted, non-live strand without asking whether its work is still pending.

Expected: after a crash, `reed resume` brings back only strands with work left, or a strand is removed from reed's state as soon as its shuttle run reaches a final outcome, independent of the waiting process.

entries.title: board: mark running tasks and refuse scope edits to them
entries.brief: The board shows which tasks have a run in flight and refuses writes that change their scope
entries.body:
A task whose run has started can still be edited on the board, and nothing tells a writer that it is running.
On 2026-10-06 the orch folded two new issues into `bugfix-sessions` with `lyx board intake import --into` while that run sat planned and parked before Webster, so the board entry no longer matched the plan its run was executing.

Wanted (operator, 2026-10-06):
- The board marks which tasks are active, from the moment their run starts until it lands or is abandoned, and `lyx board list --text` and the README show the marker.
- A write that changes an active task's scope (body, brief, issues, labels, a merge or an intake `into`) is refused with the reason, naming the run.
  Where new findings go instead: a note of their own, or the next bugfix bucket.

entries.title: Recovery prompt gives no guidance on uncommitted changes left by the prior attempt
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #406](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/406).

A recovery run for a Webster task segment was started with the reason `none` and an instruction to continue from the committed tree.
The worktree nevertheless held a large uncommitted body of work from the earlier attempt (dozens of files, thousands of changed lines).
The recovery prompt did not mention these changes or say whether to trust and keep them or to discard them, so the agent had to judge on its own whether the earlier work was sound.

This is abnormal because the recovery prompt contradicts the worktree state: "continue from the committed tree" is not true when the tree is dirty.
The agent kept the work only after verifying it independently (build, both test tiers, a fresh rerun of the segment's check).

Suggested fix: when lyx starts a recovery, have it detect uncommitted changes in the worktree and name them in the recovery prompt, together with an explicit keep-or-discard instruction.

Provenance: task `test-suite-prune-core`; note `10-websterengine-prune-recovery.md`.
